a: Notaphily is the study and collection of paper money and banknotes, a specialized branch of numismatics that has grown significantly since the 1970s as collectors recognized the historical and artistic value of banknotes alongside their monetary significance. Paper money originated in 7th-century China during the Tang Dynasty, with the first government-issued paper currency appearing under the Song Dynasty, but the practice did not reach Europe until 1661 when the Stockholm Banco in Sweden issued the first European banknotes. US paper money history includes several distinct types: Gold Certificates (redeemable in gold, issued 1863-1933), Silver Certificates (redeemable in silver, issued 1878-1964 with the last certificate, the 1957 $1, redeemable until 1968), Legal Tender Notes or United States Notes (the first national paper currency, authorized by the Legal Tender Act of 1862), Federal Reserve Notes (the current US currency, first issued in 1914), and National Bank Notes (issued by individual chartered banks from 1863 to 1935, backed by US government bonds and now highly collectible for their variety of issuing banks and signatures).

q: What are the security features of modern banknotes?
How are banknotes designed with security in mind?
What is intaglio printing on banknotes?
What are watermarks on banknotes?
What are security threads in banknotes?
What are holograms on banknotes?
What are color-shifting inks?
What is microprinting on banknotes?
What are star notes and replacement notes?
What are error notes in paper money collecting?
banknote security features design intaglio watermark
star notes replacement notes error notes varieties
a: Modern banknotes incorporate multiple security features designed to prevent counterfeiting and enable quick authentication: intaglio printing (raised ink that can be felt, created by engraved plates under high pressure), watermarks (subtle designs visible when held to light, created by varying paper thickness during manufacturing), security threads (embedded polymer or metal strips that appear as continuous or broken lines when held to light, often with microprinted text), and holograms or optically variable devices that shift appearance when tilted. Color-shifting ink changes color depending on the viewing angle, microprinting appears as a solid line to the naked eye but reveals tiny text under magnification, and see-through registers align perfectly when the note is held to light. Collectors seek specialty notes including star notes (replacement notes with a star symbol in the serial number, printed to replace misprinted notes in a run, typically rarer than regular issues), error notes (featuring printing mistakes like miscuts, misregistration, missing overprints, double denominations, or wrong colors), and fancy serial numbers (repeating digits, ladders, radars, or low numbers).

a: Major world banknote series include the Euro series (the first Europa series 2013-2019 introduced enhanced security and a portrait watermark, replacing the original 2002 series), British pound series (the current polymer Series G featuring polymer £5 with Churchill, £10 with Austen, £20 with Turner, and £50 with Turing), US dollar series (the current notes are from the Series 1996 and later with enlarged off-center portraits and security threads), Canadian Journey and Frontier series (Canada was an early adopter of polymer notes, beginning with the $100 note in 2011 and completing all denominations by 2013). Polymer banknotes, pioneered by Australia in 1988 for the bicentennial $10 note, offer superior durability (lasting 2.5-4 times longer than paper), enhanced security features (transparent windows, embossed tactile features for the visually impaired), and resistance to dirt and moisture, with over 30 countries now using polymer or hybrid substrates, including the UK, Canada, Australia, New Zealand, Singapore, Vietnam, and Mexico.

a: Hyperinflation notes are among the most dramatic and collectible paper money issues, with the most famous being Weimar Germany's 1923 100 trillion mark note (worth about 50 US cents at issue), Hungary's 1946 100 million billion (10^20) pengő note (the highest face value banknote ever issued), Zimbabwe's 2008 $100 trillion note (which briefly purchased only a loaf of bread), and Yugoslavia's 1993 500 billion dinar note. Notgeld (German for emergency money) was issued by cities, towns, and private businesses during the hyperinflation period and is highly collectible for its extraordinary variety of designs, often featuring local landmarks, folklore, and satirical artwork. Military payment certificates (MPC) were used by US armed forces from 1946 to 1973 to control local economies during deployments, while occupation currency and invasion currency were issued by occupying powers and are collected alongside Allied Military Currency, invasion scrip, and prisoner of war camp money, with collectors using catalogs like the Standard Catalog of World Paper Money (Albert Pick) and specialized references.
